en: Itivuttaka 30 Dukanipāta, Paṭhamavagga Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard: “Monks, there are these two kinds of persons found existing in the world. What two? The one who is a speaker of what has been seen, and the one who is a speaker of what has not been seen. These, monks, are the two kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, a certain monk approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that monk said to the Blessed One: “How is it, venerable sir, that one is a speaker of what has been seen, and how is it that one is a speaker of what has not been seen? “Here, monk, someone says: ‘I saw this,’ or ‘I heard this. If what he says is true and not false, then he is a speaker of what has been seen. And here, monk, someone says: ‘I did not see this,’ or ‘I did not hear this. If what he says is true and not false, then he is a speaker of what has not been seen. It is in this way, monk, that one is a speaker of what has been seen, and in this way that one is a speaker of what has not been seen. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, that monk approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that monk said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Just now, friend Ānanda, I approached the Blessed One and asked him: ‘How is it, venerable sir, that one is a speaker of what has been seen, and how is it that one is a speaker of what has not been seen? The Venerable Ānanda replied: ‘In this case, friend, someone says: “I saw this,” or “I heard this. If what he says is true and not false, then he is a speaker of what has been seen. And in this case, friend, someone says: “I did not see this,” or “I did not hear this. If what he says is true and not false, then he is a speaker of what has not been seen. It is in this way, friend, that one is a speaker of what has been seen, and in this way that one is a speaker of what has not been seen. “It is wonderful, friend Ānanda! It is marvelous, friend Ānanda! How well this was stated by the Venerable Ānanda, and how well it accords with the Dhamma. The Discourse on That Which Causes Torment.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; thus have I heard:
"Bhikkhus, there are these two things that cause torment."
Here, monks, a certain person has not done what is good, has not done what is wholesome, has not provided a refuge for those in fear; he has done evil, done what is cruel, done what is sinful.
He burns with the thought, "I have not done what is good," and he burns with the thought, "I have done what is evil."
Thus the Blessed One spoke. With regard to this, it is said:
And whatever else is associated with hatred—
having failed to perform wholesome karma and having performed much unwholesome karma;
"With the breakup of the body, the one of poor wisdom is reborn in hell.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
